city.caveat: This is the official city record as kept, without adjustments. It joins several observing sites over the years, and a move, a new instrument or the city growing around a station can shift readings (city growth mostly warms nights); NOAA's adjusted climate datasets correct for these. Treat any single number as approximate.

text.p_yest: The high of 50°F was typical for November 13. The normal high for the date is 57°F, and the record is 77°F (1955). The low of 38°F was typical for November 13.
text.t_rec: Baltimore is setting record highs far faster than chance
text.p_rec: If Baltimore's climate weren't changing, every year would have the same chance of holding a daily record. Since 2000, Baltimore has set 52 standing record lows, close to the 64 that chance alone would give, and 96 record highs, far more than the 64 that chance alone would give. The 2010s hold the most record highs of any decade (42). Baltimore's all-time high is 107°F, on July 10, 1936.
text.t_chg: Baltimore's nights cooled over the long run but have warmed since 1986. Its days have warmed.
text.p_chg: Across 153 complete years: Baltimore's average low has fallen −0.12°F per decade (95% range −0.18 to −0.06), about −1.9°F since 1873. Baltimore's average high has risen +0.26°F per decade (95% range +0.21 to +0.30), about +3.9°F since 1873. The last 40 years tell a different story: since 1986, lows have risen +0.68°F per decade (95% range +0.35 to +0.99) and highs have risen +0.63°F per decade (95% range +0.20 to +1.06). The full record joins different observing sites over the years, and a move (for example, from the city to a cooler airport) can hide or exaggerate a long-run trend, so the recent decades are the clearer guide here.
text.t_mon: Lows rose in none; 8 months fell. Highs rose in 11 of 12 months.

text.p_rain: Baltimore's yearly precipitation shows no clear long-term change (+0.08 inches per decade, a range that includes zero). The 1991–2020 normal is 45.0 inches a year. The wettest year was 2018 (71.82 in); the driest, 1930 (21.55 in).
